The audit layer writes a durable record for every secret operation: who accessed which key, when it happened, and whether it succeeded. It is separate from logging and metrics: Concern Purpose Retention Logging Operator diagnostics Short, sampled Metrics Aggregates and alerts Time series Audit trail Per-access compliance record Long, durable Audit records never contain a secret value. Failed operations record the exception type, not the exception message, because backend messages can echo the submitted payload.

await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithVault(options => { options.Url = "https://vault:8200"; options.Token = token; }) .WithAudit(options => { options.Sinks.Add(new FileSecretAuditSink("/var/log/secrets-audit.jsonl")); options.Scope = SecretAuditScope.All; options.OnSinkFailure = AuditFailureMode.Ignore; options.OnSinkError = ex => logger.LogError(ex, "audit sink failed"); }) .Build(); WithAuditSink is the shorthand when only a sink is needed: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets") .WithAuditSink(new FileSecretAuditSink("/var/log/secrets-audit.jsonl")) .Build(); The builder fills in the registered provider name automatically. Records contain: Property Description Operation GetSecretAsync, PutSecretAsync, DeleteSecretAsync, GetSecretVersionsAsync, SecretExistsAsync, or DisposeAsync Provider Registered provider name, for example vault or postgresql Key Target secret key, when the operation targets one Version Resolved version, when the operation returns one Outcome Success, Failure, Cancelled, or Denied Timestamp Operation start time, captured by the library Duration How long the operation took ActorId / ActorDisplayName Identity from the ambient actor accessor CorrelationId From Activity baggage, when the host set correlation.id or correlation-id TraceId Current Activity trace id FailureType Exception type name when the operation failed

Scope selects which operations are audited. The default is All. .WithAudit(options => { options.Scope = SecretAuditScope.Reads | SecretAuditScope.Deletes; }) Value Operations Reads GetSecretAsync Writes PutSecretAsync Deletes DeleteSecretAsync Enumeration GetSecretVersionsAsync, SecretExistsAsync All Everything above, plus DisposeAsync SecretExistsAsync and GetSecretVersionsAsync are treated as enumeration because they reveal secret names even when they do not reveal values.

The library cannot infer the caller. Push an actor per request or message scope: public sealed class SecretActorMiddleware(RequestDelegate next) { public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, ISecretActorAccessor accessor) { using var _ = accessor.Push(new SecretActor( Id: context.User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value ?? "anonymous", DisplayName: context.User.Identity?.Name)); await next(context); } } The default accessor is AmbientSecretActorAccessor.Instance, which flows the actor through AsyncLocal<T>, so it follows async continuations. AddSecretsManager registers that instance as ISecretActorAccessor in DI. Set AuditLayerOptions.ActorAccessor to use a different implementation.

By default, a broken sink never changes the outcome of a secret operation: Every sink call is wrapped. Sink errors go to OnSinkError; they do not propagate. Audit writes use CancellationToken.None, so a record is still written when the caller cancels. On a failed operation the original exception is always rethrown, even with OnSinkFailure = AuditFailureMode.Throw. Set OnSinkFailure = AuditFailureMode.Throw only when the audit trail is a hard requirement, and document the resulting outage risk. It is not the default. Every registered sink still receives the record before the failure is rethrown. warning Audit records are written after the provider operation completes. For PutSecretAsync and DeleteSecretAsync with Throw, a sink failure is reported to the caller even though the mutation has already committed. An outer retry layer may then repeat that mutation. Reads are fail-closed because the value is not returned.

The audit layer records the call it wraps. Placing it outside WithRetry records one event per logical call; placing it inside records one event per retry attempt. Choose the position deliberately and keep it stable across services.

FileSecretAuditSink writes one JSON object per line (JSON Lines), append-only. var sink = new FileSecretAuditSink("/var/log/secrets-audit.jsonl", new FileSecretAuditSinkOptions { FlushEachWrite = true, MaxFileSizeBytes = 100 * 1024 * 1024 }); Option Type Required Default Description FlushEachWrite bool No true Force each record to durable storage. An unflushed audit record is not an audit record MaxFileSizeBytes long? No null Rotate to <name>.<UTC timestamp><extension> when the file reaches this size, for example audit.20261021T1200000000000.jsonl. Rotated files are never overwritten or deleted The parent directory is created when it does not exist. On Unix, a newly created sink file is opened with 0600 permissions. Rotation keeps the extension, so *.jsonl globs still find rotated files. Retention is the host's responsibility: rotated files are never deleted.

The mrhamburg.SecretsManager.PostgreSql package ships PostgreSqlSecretAuditSink: Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; }) .WithPostgreSqlAuditSink(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; options.Schema = "public"; options.TableName = "sm_secret_audit_log"; }) .Build(); Option Type Required Default Description ConnectionString string Yes "" PostgreSQL connection string Schema string No "public" Schema for the audit table TableName string No "sm_secret_audit_log" Audit table name AutoCreateSchema bool No false Create the table and timestamp index on first write. Requires CREATE on the schema Schema and TableName must be letters, digits, or underscores and start with a letter or underscore. TableName is capped at 48 characters so the generated <table>_timestamp_idx index name fits PostgreSQL's 63-character identifier limit. With AutoCreateSchema = false, create the table from a migration role: CREATE TABLE public.sm_secret_audit_log ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, "timestamp" TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, "operation" TEXT NOT NULL, "provider" TEXT NOT NULL, "key" TEXT, "version" TEXT, "outcome" TEXT NOT NULL, "duration_ms" DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, "actor_id" TEXT, "actor_display_name" TEXT, "correlation_id" TEXT, "trace_id" TEXT, "failure_type" TEXT ); CREATE INDEX sm_secret_audit_log_timestamp_idx ON public.sm_secret_audit_log ("timestamp"); GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON public.sm_secret_audit_log TO secrets_app; GRANT USAGE ON SEQUENCE public.sm_secret_audit_log_id_seq TO secrets_app; The sink stores Outcome as text (Success, Failure, Cancelled, Denied) and Duration as milliseconds. It uses the same Npgsql connection string conventions as the PostgreSQL provider; add SSL Mode=VerifyFull when the database is not a trusted local socket.

Sinks are objects, so they cannot come from appsettings.json. The policy can: { "SecretsManager": { "Audit": { "Enabled": true, "Scope": "All", "OnSinkFailure": "Ignore" } } } var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .ConfigurePostgreSql(configuration) .ConfigureAudit(configuration) .WithPostgreSqlAuditSink(options => { options.ConnectionString = configuration.GetConnectionString("Audit")!; }) .Build(); ConfigureAudit adds the layer with the policy from configuration. A sink must still be registered with WithAuditSink or WithPostgreSqlAuditSink. Build fails when the layer is enabled and has no sinks.

Implement ISecretAuditSink. Implementations must be thread-safe: public sealed class MyAuditSink : ISecretAuditSink { public ValueTask WriteAsync( SecretAuditEvent auditEvent, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) { // Forward to your SIEM or database. return ValueTask.CompletedTask; } } The interface is deliberately small so database and SIEM connectors stay consumer-provided unless a package ships one, as mrhamburg.SecretsManager.PostgreSql does.
SecretsManager is designed to be extensible. You can implement your own provider for any secret backend.

Create a class that implements the ISecretProvider interface: MyCustomSecretProvider.cs using SecretsManager; public class MyCustomSecretProvider : ISecretProvider { public async Task<SecretValue> GetSecretAsync( string key, SecretQuery? query = null, CancellationToken ct = default) { // Retrieve secret from your backend var value = await YourBackend.GetAsync(key, ct); return new SecretValue(key, value); } public async Task<SecretValue> PutSecretAsync( string key, string value, SecretMetadata? metadata = null, CancellationToken ct = default) { await YourBackend.SetAsync(key, value, ct); return new SecretValue(key, value); } public async Task DeleteSecretAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct = default) { await YourBackend.DeleteAsync(key, ct); } public async Task<IReadOnlyList<SecretVersionInfo>> GetSecretVersionsAsync( string key, CancellationToken ct = default) { return await YourBackend.ListVersionsAsync(key, ct); } public async Task<bool> SecretExistsAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct = default) { return await YourBackend.ExistsAsync(key, ct); } public ValueTask DisposeAsync() { // Clean up resources return ValueTask.CompletedTask; } }

To integrate with the builder pattern, implement ISecretProviderFactory: MyCustomSecretProviderFactory.cs using SecretsManager.Builder; public class MyCustomSecretProviderFactory : ISecretProviderFactory { public string ProviderName => "mycustom"; public ISecretProvider Create(Dictionary<string, string> settings) { var endpoint = settings["endpoint"]; var apiKey = settings["apiKey"]; return new MyCustomSecretProvider(endpoint, apiKey); } }

Create a fluent extension method: SecretProviderBuilderExtensions.cs public static class SecretProviderBuilderExtensions { public static SecretProviderBuilder WithMyCustom( this SecretProviderBuilder builder, Action<MyCustomOptions>? configure = null) { builder.RegisterFactory(new MyCustomSecretProviderFactory()); if (configure != null) { var options = new MyCustomOptions(); configure(options); builder.ApplyOptions(options); } return builder; } } tip Follow the existing provider implementations in the repository as reference. The FileSystem provider is the simplest starting point.
SecretsManager can extract nested values from JSON-formatted secrets using dot-path syntax. This is useful when a single secret contains multiple related values.

If a secret stores a JSON object, you can extract specific properties: // Secret "db-config" contains: // {"host": "db.example.com", "port": 5432, "username": "admin", "password": "s3cret"} var query = new SecretQuery { Property = "password" }; var password = await provider.GetSecretAsync("db-config", query); Console.WriteLine(password.Value); // "s3cret"

Use dot notation to access nested values: // Secret "app-config" contains: // {"database": {"connection": {"host": "db.example.com", "port": 5432}}} var query = new SecretQuery { Property = "database.connection.host" }; var host = await provider.GetSecretAsync("app-config", query); Console.WriteLine(host.Value); // "db.example.com"

You can combine property extraction with version queries: var query = new SecretQuery { Version = "v2", Property = "database.password" }; var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("config", query); info JSON extraction is handled by the core library's JsonPropertyExtractor and works identically across all providers. The extraction happens after the secret value is retrieved from the backend.

You can compose additional behavior around any ISecretProvider by using layers. Layers are decorators that wrap a provider implementation and add cross-cutting behavior without changing the provider itself. SecretProviderBuilder applies layers in the same order they are added. using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.Builder; var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets"; }) .WithRetry() .WithTimeout() .WithLogging(options => options.OperationPrefix = "app") .Build(); In this example, Retry is applied first, then Timeout, then Logging, and finally the base provider.

Keep providers focused while adding resiliency and observability once. Build predictable call behavior across environments. Share the same policy across provider types. Reduce boilerplate for retries, throttling, tracing, and diagnostics.

The core package ships these decorators: Concurrent limiter: WithConcurrentLimiter Retry: WithRetry Timeout: WithTimeout Logging: WithLogging Audit trail: WithAudit / WithAuditSink OpenTelemetry metrics: WithOtelMetrics OpenTelemetry trace: WithOtelTrace

Limits how many provider operations run at the same time. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets") .WithConcurrentLimiter(options => { options.MaxConcurrentRequests = 5; options.AcquireTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200); }) .Build(); Options: MaxConcurrentRequests: maximum concurrent operations (default 10). AcquireTimeout: wait timeout before failing with TimeoutException (null means wait forever).

Retries failed provider calls with exponential backoff. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; }) .WithRetry(options => { options.MaxAttempts = 5; options.BaseDelay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100); options.MaxDelay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2); options.JitterFactor = 0.2; }) .Build(); Defaults: Retries only transient failures by default (timeouts, I/O and transport errors). Does not retry SecretNotFoundException, ArgumentException, or cancelled operations. Never retries PutSecretAsync, because writes are not idempotent. MaxAttempts includes the first attempt. RetryPredicate can override retry behavior.

Applies a cancellation deadline per operation. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithGoogleSecretManager(options => { options.ProjectId = "my-project"; options.CredentialsPath = "/etc/secrets/gcp.json"; }) .WithTimeout(options => { options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5); }) .Build(); Default timeout is 10 seconds.

Emits lifecycle events for each operation: start, success, failure, and retries. See Logging for the full guide. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithScaleway(options => { options.Region = "fr-par"; options.ProjectId = "..."; }) .WithRetry() .WithLogging(options => { options.OperationPrefix = "secret"; options.Logger = new LoggerSecretProviderLogger(logger); // Microsoft.Extensions.Logging }) .Build(); ISecretProviderLogger interface: public interface ISecretProviderLogger { bool IsEnabled(SecretProviderLogLevel level); void LogStart(SecretProviderLogContext context); void LogSuccess(SecretProviderLogContext context, TimeSpan duration); void LogFailure(SecretProviderLogContext context, Exception exception, TimeSpan duration); void LogRetry(SecretProviderLogContext context, int attempt, TimeSpan delay); } Event SecretProviderLogLevel MEL LogLevel Start, success Debug Debug Retry Warning Warning Failure Error Error OperationPrefix prepends operation names (for example secret.GetSecretAsync). The builder sets Provider on every event, so logs can be attributed to a backend. With WithLogging and WithRetry, each retry is logged with the attempt number and delay. A logger that throws never changes the result of a secret operation. If no logger is provided, NullSecretProviderLogger is used.

Emits a durable record per secret operation for compliance. Unlike logging, the audit layer records the actor, provider name, timestamp, outcome, and a failure type without ever recording a secret value. A broken sink does not change the secret operation's outcome by default. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets") .WithAudit(options => { options.Sinks.Add(new FileSecretAuditSink("/var/log/secrets-audit.jsonl")); options.Scope = SecretAuditScope.All; options.OnSinkFailure = AuditFailureMode.Ignore; }) .Build(); See Audit Trail for actor propagation, failure semantics, the file sink, and the PostgreSQL sink.

Generates metrics using System.Diagnostics.Metrics. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets") .WithOtelMetrics(options => { options.MeterName = "secrets.metrics"; options.MeterVersion = "1.0.0"; options.MetricPrefix = "secrets."; }) .Build(); Emitted metric names are prefixed by MetricPrefix, for example: secrets.operation.calls secrets.operation.failures secrets.operation.duration_ms secrets.operation.in_flight

Adds Activity spans for all operations. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithAwsSecretsManager(options => { options.Region = "us-east-1"; options.AccessKey = "AKIA..."; options.SecretKey = "..."; }) .WithOtelTrace(options => { options.ActivitySourceName = "my-secrets-traces"; options.RecordException = true; }) .Build(); Span tags include: secrets.operation secrets.key

You can create your own decorator by implementing ISecretProviderLayer and wrapping ISecretProvider. The example below is a pass-through; the library's real audit layer is documented in Audit Trail. public sealed class CustomLayer : ISecretProviderLayer { public ISecretProvider Wrap(ISecretProvider inner) { return new CustomProvider(inner); } private sealed class CustomProvider(ISecretProvider inner) : ISecretProvider { public Task<SecretValue> GetSecretAsync(string key, SecretQuery? query = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => inner.GetSecretAsync(key, query, cancellationToken); public Task<SecretValue> PutSecretAsync(string key, string value, SecretMetadata? metadata = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => inner.PutSecretAsync(key, value, metadata, cancellationToken); public Task DeleteSecretAsync(string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => inner.DeleteSecretAsync(key, cancellationToken); public Task<IReadOnlyList<SecretVersionInfo>> GetSecretVersionsAsync(string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => inner.GetSecretVersionsAsync(key, cancellationToken); public Task<bool> SecretExistsAsync(string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) => inner.SecretExistsAsync(key, cancellationToken); public ValueTask DisposeAsync() => inner.DisposeAsync(); } } Then call it via AddLayer: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(opts => opts.BasePath = "/etc/secrets") .AddLayer(new CustomLayer()) .Build(); Or create a small extension method in your own project.

Layers wrap a finished provider, so they can change what a call does, but not what the provider is. Encryption is the clearest example. SecretProviderBuilder.Build() constructs the provider first and wraps it afterwards: var provider = factory.Create(_configuration.Settings); // options read here for (var i = _layers.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--) provider = _layers[i].Wrap(provider); // layers wrap AFTER A layer receives only the finished provider. The key source is a property of the provider's options, and the provider's options are not reachable from the wrapped interface — the layer has no reference to them, or to the provider's internals. A decorator can intercept calls, but it cannot reach back into the configuration that produced the provider. The only way a layer could work is if the provider exposed its key source for replacement — which would mean publishing key material through a public API, the opposite of what encryption is for. Sourcing the key from another provider therefore lives in the providers' key resolution, not in the layer pipeline. See FileSystem Provider and PostgreSql Provider for EncryptionKeyProvider and SecretProviderKeySource. note The key itself is resolved lazily, on first use, rather than at construction time — a key held in another provider may require a network round trip. That does not make it layerable: the source of the key is fixed when the provider is built, which is before any layer runs.

documents.t: LoggingLayer reports every secret operation to an ISecretProviderLogger. The built-in LoggerSecretProviderLogger adapts that interface to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, so secret operations appear in the same sinks as the rest of your application (console, Seq, Elastic, Loki, OpenTelemetry log export, and so on). Logging lives in a layer, not in the providers. No provider constructor takes a logger, so all 14 provider packages keep their public API. The layer also sees pipeline behavior that a provider cannot see, such as retries.

using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging; using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.Builder; ILogger logger = loggerFactory.CreateLogger("SecretsManager"); await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/var/secrets") .WithLogging(options => { options.Logger = new LoggerSecretProviderLogger(logger); options.OperationPrefix = "app"; }) .Build();

AddSecretsManager() registers an ISecretProviderLogger that writes through the application's ILoggerFactory (category SecretsManager). When no ILoggerFactory is registered, it falls back to a no-op logger. A logger that you register yourself is never replaced. builder.Services.AddLogging(); builder.Services.AddSecretsManager(); builder.Services.AddSingleton<ISecretProvider>(sp => { var secrets = sp.GetRequiredService<SecretProviderBuilder>(); return secrets .WithFileSystem(options => options.BasePath = "/var/secrets") .WithRetry() .WithLogging(sp.GetRequiredService<ISecretProviderLogger>()) .Build(); });

The adapter honors the minimum level of your logging configuration. The layer asks IsEnabled first, so when a level is filtered out it builds no context and makes no logger call. Event SecretProviderLogLevel MEL LogLevel Operation start Debug Debug Operation success Debug Debug Retry Warning Warning Operation failure Error Error

Every event receives a SecretProviderLogContext. Field Description Operation Operation name, for example GetSecretAsync, with the optional OperationPrefix Key Secret key IsMetadataWrite Whether a write carries metadata Provider Provider name, for example vault. The builder sets it on every layer Outcome Success or Failure. It is null for the start event Timestamp When the operation started The MEL adapter writes Operation, Key and Provider as structured properties, plus ElapsedMs for success and failure, and Attempt and DelayMs for retries.

When a RetryLayer retries a read, the logger receives a LogRetry event with the next attempt number and the delay. Add WithLogging and WithRetry in either order. The builder shares the logging layer's logger with the retry layer. Set RetryLayerOptions.Logger to use a different one.

Logging is best-effort. A logger that throws, in any method including IsEnabled, cannot: fail a secret operation, turn a successful read into a failure, hide the original exception of a failed operation. The layer swallows logger exceptions.

SecretProviderLogContext has no value field, and secret values are never logged. Secret keys are logged. The providers with a REST client (Aliyun KMS, Conjur, IBM Cloud Secrets Manager, OVH, Passbolt, Scaleway, Tencent Cloud and Vault) do not copy the response body into exception messages. Their error messages contain only the operation, HTTP status code and reason phrase, because backends can echo submitted values in error payloads. If an exception from PutSecretAsync still contains the submitted value, the layer replaces it with [REDACTED] before it is logged. The caller still receives the original exception. Exception messages that come from other sources, such as provider SDKs, are logged as they are. OtelTraceLayer also records exception messages in its spans. Treat your log and trace sinks as sensitive.
When the caller cancels an operation through its CancellationToken, the layer does not log it as a failure. Other exceptions, including SecretNotFoundException, are logged at Error.

Implement ISecretProviderLogger to send events to another destination: public interface ISecretProviderLogger { bool IsEnabled(SecretProviderLogLevel level); void LogStart(SecretProviderLogContext context); void LogSuccess(SecretProviderLogContext context, TimeSpan duration); void LogFailure(SecretProviderLogContext context, Exception exception, TimeSpan duration); void LogRetry(SecretProviderLogContext context, int attempt, TimeSpan delay); } IsEnabled and LogRetry have default implementations (true and no-op), so a logger that implements only LogStart, LogSuccess and LogFailure keeps working. NullSecretProviderLogger is the default and emits nothing.
All SecretsManager providers support secret versioning, allowing you to maintain a complete history of secret values.

Every call to PutSecretAsync creates a new version of the secret. The latest version is always returned by default when calling GetSecretAsync. // Create initial version await provider.PutSecretAsync("db-password", "initial-password"); // Update creates a new version await provider.PutSecretAsync("db-password", "updated-password"); // Gets the latest version by default var current = await provider.GetSecretAsync("db-password"); Console.WriteLine(current.Value); // "updated-password"

Use GetSecretVersionsAsync to retrieve the full version history: var versions = await provider.GetSecretVersionsAsync("db-password"); foreach (var version in versions) { Console.WriteLine($"Version: {version.Version}"); Console.WriteLine($"Created: {version.CreatedAt}"); }

Pass a SecretQuery with the version identifier to retrieve a historical value: var query = new SecretQuery { Version = "v1" }; var oldSecret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("db-password", query); Console.WriteLine(oldSecret.Value); // "initial-password" tip Version identifiers vary by provider. FileSystem uses v1, v2, etc. Azure Key Vault uses Azure-generated version IDs. Scaleway uses revision numbers. The GetSecretVersionsAsync method returns the correct identifiers for each provider.
Provider Version Format Auto-Versioning Max Versions FileSystem v1, v2, v3... Yes Unlimited Azure Key Vault Azure GUID Yes Unlimited Scaleway Revision number Yes Unlimited

The core interface that all providers implement. public interface ISecretProvider : IAsyncDisposable { Task<SecretValue> GetSecretAsync( string key, SecretQuery? query = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); Task<SecretValue> PutSecretAsync( string key, string value, SecretMetadata? metadata = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); Task DeleteSecretAsync( string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); Task<IReadOnlyList<SecretVersionInfo>> GetSecretVersionsAsync( string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); Task<bool> SecretExistsAsync( string key, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); }

Represents a retrieved secret with its value and metadata. Property Type Description Key string The secret's key/name Value string The secret's value Version string? Version identifier CreatedAt DateTimeOffset? When this version was created ContentType string? MIME type of the value
Options for retrieving secrets. Property Type Description Version string? Specific version to retrieve Property string? JSON dot-path to extract a nested value
Write-side metadata for creating or updating secrets. Property Type Description ContentType string? MIME type of the value Tags Dictionary<string, string>? Key-value tags/labels
Information about a single version of a secret. Property Type Description Version string Version identifier CreatedAt DateTimeOffset When this version was created

Thrown when a requested secret does not exist. try { var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("nonexistent-key"); } catch (SecretNotFoundException ex) { Console.WriteLine($"Secret not found: {ex.SecretKey}"); }
Base exception for provider-specific errors (network failures, auth errors, etc.).

Fluent builder for configuring and creating providers. var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { /* ... */ }) // or WithAzureKeyVault, WithScaleway, WithPostgreSql, WithInfisical .FromEnvironment() // optional: load from env vars .FromYamlFile("secretstore.yaml") // optional: load from YAML .Build(); // returns ISecretProvider

Layers are decorators that wrap providers and can add cross-cutting behavior. public interface ISecretProviderLayer { ISecretProvider Wrap(ISecretProvider inner); } public sealed class SecretProviderBuilder { public SecretProviderBuilder AddLayer(ISecretProviderLayer layer); }

Layer builders are in the SecretsManager.Builder namespace: using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.Builder; var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { /* ... */ }) .WithConcurrentLimiter() // controls max concurrent operations .WithRetry() // retries transient failures .WithTimeout() // per-operation timeout .WithLogging() // start/success/failure/retry logging .WithAudit() // durable per-access audit records .WithOtelMetrics() // emits System.Diagnostics.Metrics .WithOtelTrace() // emits OpenTelemetry Activity spans .Build(); All layers support optional options callbacks, for example: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { /* ... */ }) .WithRetry(options => options.MaxAttempts = 5) .WithTimeout(options => options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)) .WithConcurrentLimiter(options => options.MaxConcurrentRequests = 10) .WithOtelMetrics(options => options.MeterName = "secrets-metrics") .WithOtelTrace(options => options.ActivitySourceName = "secrets-traces") .Build();

LoggingLayer writes events to an ISecretProviderLogger. See Logging. Type Description ISecretProviderLogger Log sink with IsEnabled, LogStart, LogSuccess, LogFailure and LogRetry LoggerSecretProviderLogger Adapter that writes to a Microsoft.Extensions.Logging ILogger NullSecretProviderLogger No-op default SecretProviderLogContext Operation, key, provider, outcome and timestamp. It never holds a secret value SecretProviderLogLevel Debug, Information, Warning or Error SecretProviderLogOutcome Success or Failure

AuditLayer writes a SecretAuditEvent to one or more ISecretAuditSink instances. Type Description SecretAuditEvent Immutable record: operation, provider, key, version, outcome, timestamp, duration, actor, correlation id, trace id, and failure type SecretAuditOutcome Success, Failure, Cancelled, or Denied SecretAuditScope Flags that select reads, writes, deletes, enumeration, or all operations ISecretAuditSink Destination for audit records ISecretActorAccessor Ambient actor lookup, with AmbientSecretActorAccessor.Instance as the default FileSecretAuditSink JSON Lines file sink PostgreSqlSecretAuditSink PostgreSQL sink in the mrhamburg.SecretsManager.PostgreSql package See Audit Trail for usage.
SecretsManager supports four configuration approaches. Choose the one that best fits your workflow.

The most common approach for .NET applications. Configure providers directly in code: Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets"; options.EncryptionKey = "base64-encoded-key"; }) .Build(); This approach works well for: Applications with static configuration Dependency injection setups Unit testing with mock providers

For applications using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, register SecretsManager and bind configuration from IConfiguration: Program.cs using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.FileSystem; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); // Register the SecretsManager builder builder.Services.AddSecretsManager(); // Bind configuration from appsettings.json builder.Services.Configure<FileSystemOptions>( builder.Configuration.GetSection("SecretsManager:FileSystem")); Or use the ConfigureXxx(IConfiguration) bridge for a shorter form: Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .ConfigureFileSystem(builder.Configuration) .Build(); Configuration file (appsettings.json): { "SecretsManager": { "FileSystem": { "BasePath": "/etc/secrets", "EncryptionKey": "base64-encoded-key" } } } All options are validated at configuration time. Invalid values throw ArgumentException with a descriptive message. This approach works well for: ASP.NET Core applications Applications using appsettings.json with environment-specific overrides Teams that want configuration validation at startup

Configure providers through environment variables for container and cloud-native deployments: Terminal export SECRETS_PROVIDER=filesystem export SECRETS_FILESYSTEM_PATH=/etc/secrets export SECRETS_FILESYSTEM_ENCRYPTION_KEY=base64encodedkey Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem() .FromEnvironment() .Build(); This approach works well for: Docker and Kubernetes deployments CI/CD pipelines Cloud-native applications

Use External Secrets Operator-style YAML files for declarative configuration: secretstore.yaml provider: filesystem: path: /etc/secrets encryption: key: base64encodedkey Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem() .FromYamlFile("secretstore.yaml") .Build(); This approach works well for: Teams already using External Secrets Operator GitOps workflows Multi-environment configuration management Combining Sources You can combine configuration sources. For example, use YAML for base configuration and environment variables for sensitive values like encryption keys.

First, install the core library and your chosen provider. For this example, we'll use the FileSystem provider: Terminal dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.FileSystem

Configure the provider using the Fluent API. Add this to your Program.cs or startup code: Program.cs using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.Builder; using SecretsManager.FileSystem; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); // Register SecretsManager builder.Services.AddSingleton<ISecretProvider>(sp => { return new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKey = builder.Configuration["Encryption:Key"]; }) .Build(); }); var app = builder.Build(); app.Run(); You can also add resilient and observable behavior in one fluent chain: Program.cs using SecretsManager; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); builder.Services.AddSingleton<ISecretProvider>(sp => { return new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKey = builder.Configuration["Encryption:Key"]; }) .WithRetry() .WithTimeout(options => options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)) .WithLogging() .Build(); });

If you prefer the standard .NET configuration pattern, you can bind from appsettings.json: Program.cs using SecretsManager; using SecretsManager.FileSystem; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); builder.Services.AddSecretsManager(); var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .ConfigureFileSystem(builder.Configuration) .Build(); With this in appsettings.json: { "SecretsManager": { "FileSystem": { "BasePath": "/var/secrets" } } } All provider options are validated automatically. Invalid configuration throws at startup. Configuration Options You can also configure providers using environment variables or YAML files. See the Configuration guide for details.

Inject ISecretProvider into your services and start managing secrets: Controllers/SecretsController.cs using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; using SecretsManager; [ApiController] [Route("api/[controller]")] public class SecretsController : ControllerBase { private readonly ISecretProvider _secretProvider; public SecretsController(ISecretProvider secretProvider) { _secretProvider = secretProvider; } [HttpGet("{name}")] public async Task<IActionResult> GetSecret(string name) { try { var secret = await _secretProvider.GetSecretAsync(name); return Ok(new { value = secret.Value }); } catch (SecretNotFoundException) { return NotFound(); } } [HttpPost("{name}")] public async Task<IActionResult> PutSecret(string name, [FromBody] string value) { await _secretProvider.PutSecretAsync(name, value); return Ok(); } [HttpDelete("{name}")] public async Task<IActionResult> DeleteSecret(string name) { await _secretProvider.DeleteSecretAsync(name); return NoContent(); } } Best Practices Never hardcode encryption keys or credentials in your source code Use environment variables or Azure Key Vault references for sensitive configuration Enable versioning for critical secrets to maintain audit trails Implement proper error handling for SecretNotFoundException

SecretsManager is a unified .NET library that provides a consistent interface for managing secrets across multiple backend providers. Inspired by Kubernetes External Secrets Operator (ESO), it abstracts away the complexity of different secret storage solutions while maintaining full feature compatibility. Whether you're storing secrets in Azure Key Vault for production, Scaleway Secret Manager for European compliance, or encrypted local files for development, SecretsManager gives you a single API to work with. Why Unified? By using a single interface (ISecretProvider), you can swap providers without changing your business logic. This is especially useful for multi-cloud deployments or migrating between providers.

Unified API -- One interface for all providers with Get, Put, Delete, and Version operations Multi-Provider Support -- FileSystem, Azure Key Vault, Scaleway Secret Manager, and PostgreSQL Modular Design -- Install only the NuGet packages you need Versioning -- First-class support for secret history across all providers JSON Extraction -- Query nested JSON secrets using dot-path syntax Flexible Configuration -- Choose from Fluent API, Environment Variables, or YAML Layering -- Add cross-cutting behaviors like retries, timeouts, and telemetry without changing provider code

Install the core package and your chosen provider(s): Terminal # Core library dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager # Choose your provider(s) dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.FileSystem dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.AzureKeyVault dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.Scaleway dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.PostgreSql

Here's how to get started with the FileSystem provider: Program.cs using SecretsManager; // Configure the provider var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/etc/secrets"; options.EncryptionKey = "your-encryption-key"; }) .Build(); // Get a secret var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("database-password"); Console.WriteLine($"Password: {secret.Value}"); // Put a new secret await provider.PutSecretAsync("api-key", "sk-1234567890"); // Get secret with version history var versions = await provider.GetSecretVersionsAsync("api-key"); foreach (var version in versions) { Console.WriteLine($"Version {version.Version}: {version.CreatedAt}"); } Next Steps Continue to the Quick Start guide to learn how to configure different providers and explore advanced features. You can also read the Layering docs to add built-in and custom policy layers.

Aliyun KMS uses AccessKey-based authentication with HMAC-SHA1 request signing. You'll need: Region — the Alibaba Cloud region ID (e.g. cn-hangzhou, ap-southeast-1) AccessKey ID — your Alibaba Cloud AccessKey ID AccessKey Secret — your Alibaba Cloud AccessKey Secret

Log in to the Alibaba Cloud Console Navigate to RAM (Resource Access Management) Create or select a RAM user Generate an AccessKey pair under the user's security settings Grant the RAM user the AliyunKMSFullAccess policy warning Never commit your AccessKey secret to version control. Use environment variables or a secrets manager for production deployments.

The provider maps Aliyun KMS concepts to the ISecretProvider interface: ISecretProvider Aliyun KMS Secret key Secret name Secret value SecretData (server-side encrypted) Version VersionId (UUID-based, auto-generated) Metadata Not directly mapped

The provider creates Generic secrets by default. Aliyun KMS supports several secret types (Generic, Rds, Redis, RAMCredentials, ECS), but only Generic secrets support manual version management via PutSecretValue.

Aliyun KMS supports up to 10 versions per generic secret. When the limit is reached, the oldest version is automatically deleted in a rolling manner. Each version is labeled with ACSCurrent (latest) or ACSPrevious (previous).
All secret values are encrypted server-side by KMS using a symmetric key. The encryption is transparent — you work with plaintext values, and KMS handles encryption/decryption automatically.

Writing secrets: Conjur requires a variable to exist in policy before a value can be set. The provider checks for the variable and, if missing, loads a !variable policy entry into the configured policy path automatically. Set PolicyPath to the branch that owns your variables (default root). Reading secrets: Secrets are retrieved by their full identifier (e.g. app/db-pass). Conjur keeps up to 20 versions per variable. Deleting secrets: Conjur has no REST delete endpoint. Deletion is performed by patching the configured policy path with a !delete statement, which requires the update privilege on the containing policy. Nested variables: For variables declared inside a policy branch, set PolicyPath to that branch; the leading branch segment is stripped when the provider creates missing variables.

The FileSystem provider stores secrets locally with optional AES-256-GCM encryption. It's ideal for local development, edge deployments, and air-gapped environments where cloud connectivity isn't available. Key Benefits: Zero external dependencies -- works completely offline AES-256-GCM encryption at rest Built-in versioning with atomic writes Per-key file locking for concurrent access safety
Terminal dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.FileSystem

Option Type Required Default Description BasePath string Yes {LocalApplicationData}/SecretsManager Root directory where secrets are stored. Each secret gets a subdirectory EncryptionKey string? No null Base64-encoded AES-256 key (32 bytes). When set, secrets are encrypted at rest EncryptionKeyFile string? No null Path to a file containing the raw or base64-encoded AES-256 key EncryptionKeyProvider IEncryptionKeyProvider? No null Supplies the encryption key from an external source, for example another secret provider. Fluent API only — it is an object, so it cannot come from appsettings.json, YAML, or an environment variable FileSystemOptions.Validate() requires BasePath. EncryptionKey, EncryptionKeyFile and EncryptionKeyProvider are mutually exclusive — setting more than one is a validation error. With no key source set at all, secrets are stored in plaintext (development only). Secret keys are validated before any filesystem access: an empty key, or a key of . or .., is rejected with ArgumentException. Version identifiers must match v<number> (for example v1); anything else — including current, a path separator, or an absolute path — is rejected the same way. Both checks exist because a key or version previously reached the filesystem unchecked, letting ../other-secret/v1 read a different secret and . resolve to the store root.
Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKey = "base64-encoded-256-bit-key"; }) .Build();
var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKeyFile = "/etc/secrets/master.key"; }) .Build();

The key can be held in a different secret provider entirely — Scaleway, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or any of the other providers. The key is fetched on first use and cached per key version, so the steady-state cost is one read per version, not one per operation. Program.cs // The bootstrap provider holds the key. It is built first and owned by the caller. await using var keyProvider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithScaleway(options => { options.Region = "fr-par"; options.ProjectId = "..."; options.AccessKey = "..."; options.SecretKey = "..."; }) .Build(); await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKeyProvider = new SecretProviderKeySource(keyProvider, "sm/data-key"); }) .Build(); Store the key as base64 — openssl rand -base64 32 — in a secret named sm/data-key. Rotating it is a single PutSecretAsync at the source, but note that the current key is cached per process: new writes pick up the new version when the process restarts, or immediately if you call InvalidateKey(). Existing values stay readable either way, because each envelope records the key version it was written with and GetKeyAsync fetches that exact version on demand. No keyring list and no separate rotation step. WarmUpAsync() and InvalidateKey() are declared on the concrete provider types, not on ISecretProvider, so they are unavailable once a layer wraps the provider. The same pattern works with Azure Key Vault: await using var keyProvider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithAzureKeyVault(options => options.VaultUri = "https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/") .Build(); await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/var/secrets"; options.EncryptionKeyProvider = new SecretProviderKeySource(keyProvider, "sm-data-key"); }) .Build(); warning Build the key provider first, and never point a key source at the store it encrypts. A self-referential key source recurses or fails on first use — the fetch happens inside the operation that needs the key, so it cannot bootstrap itself. The key id is derived from the version the source reports ({key}@{version}), so the source must report a distinct, immutable version for every key it serves. A source whose version does not change on rotation — Passbolt always reports 1 — cannot be used as a key source: SecretProviderKeySource throws rather than silently reusing a key id, which would make values written under the previous key unreadable. SecretProviderKeySource does not dispose the provider it wraps. The caller owns the bootstrap provider and may use it for other keys. tip Call WarmUpAsync() to resolve the key (and, for PostgreSQL, ensure the schema) at startup rather than on the first read or write. Without it, a misconfigured key source surfaces only when the first secret is accessed.

documents.t: secretstore.yaml provider: filesystem: path: /var/secrets encryption: key: base64encodedkey # or: keyFile: /etc/secrets/master.key

For development only, you can disable encryption: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithFileSystem(options => { options.BasePath = "/tmp/dev-secrets"; // No encryption key = plaintext storage }) .Build(); warning Never use unencrypted mode in production. Always provide an encryption key for any environment that handles real secrets. Unencrypted mode stores values in cleartext JSON on disk with no integrity protection: anyone who can write to the store can change a secret's value undetectably. Once an encryption key is configured, the provider refuses to read any envelope stored unencrypted, and refuses to read an encrypted envelope when no key is configured. Both cases throw SecretProviderException rather than returning a value. Migrating an existing unencrypted store therefore means rewriting every secret, not just adding a key.

Secrets are stored under basePath/{key}/ with per-version JSON files: basePath/ my-secret/ current.json -> { "version": "v3" } v1.json -> VersionedSecretEnvelope (encrypted) v2.json v3.json Each version file contains the encrypted payload, metadata, and timestamp. The current.json pointer enables atomic version switching.

There is no hard rate limit enforced by the API. However, as request rate increases, some performance degradation is expected. Recommended maximum: ~20 requests per second. When rate limits are exceeded, the API responds with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Implement exponential backoff in your client when you encounter 429 responses.

The IBM Cloud Secrets Manager API uses standard HTTP status codes. All error responses share a consistent JSON structure: { "trace": "f9d9d161-e087-4871-963b-88ea3fe72aca", "status_code": 400, "errors": [ { "code": "bad_request", "message": "required.name: property \"name\" is missing", "more_info": "https://cloud.ibm.com/apidocs/secrets-manager" } ] }

The provider uses Universal Auth with a machine identity. Create the identity in the Infisical organization, attach Universal Auth, and create a client secret: Create an organization-scoped machine identity and grant it a project role. Attach Universal Auth to the identity. Create a client secret and copy the client ID and client secret. Set ProjectId, EnvironmentSlug and SecretPath to the project, environment and folder that contain the secrets. Organization-scoped identities can be added to a project with a project membership. Project-scoped identities already belong to one project and cannot be added through the project membership endpoint. warning Treat client secrets like passwords. Use environment variables or a secret manager to inject them at runtime, and grant the identity only the project role it needs.

Run a standalone Infisical instance with PostgreSQL and Redis: Terminal docker network create infisical docker run -d --name infisical-db --network infisical \ -e POSTGRES_USER=infisical -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=infisical \ -e POSTGRES_DB=infisical postgres:18 docker run -d --name infisical-redis --network infisical redis:7-alpine docker run -d --name infisical --network infisical -p 8080:8080 \ -e ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \ -e AUTH_SECRET=$(openssl rand -base64 32) \ -e DB_CONNECTION_URI=postgres://infisical:infisical@infisical-db:5432/infisical \ -e REDIS_URL=redis://infisical-redis:6379 \ -e SITE_URL=http://localhost:8080 \ infisical/infisical:v0.167.4 Wait for http://localhost:8080/api/status, then bootstrap the instance: Terminal curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/bootstrap \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"your-password","organization":"integration"}' The response contains the admin machine identity token and the organization ID. Use that token to create the project, the organization-scoped identity, the Universal Auth client, and the project membership.

// Standard ISecretProvider operations work identically var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("my-secret"); await provider.PutSecretAsync("new-secret", "secret-value"); var versions = await provider.GetSecretVersionsAsync("my-secret"); await provider.DeleteSecretAsync("old-secret");

ISecretProvider Infisical Secret key Secret name Secret value Secret value Version Numeric secret version SecretMetadata.Tags Per-secret metadata (secretMetadata). null leaves existing metadata unchanged and an empty dictionary clears it SecretMetadata.ContentType Not supported SecretValue.CreatedAt / UpdatedAt Not exposed by the .NET SDK

Version selection: SecretQuery.Version must be a positive integer. A non-numeric, zero, or negative version throws SecretProviderException. Version listing: The .NET SDK has no version-list endpoint, and the enterprise version-history endpoint is not reachable with Universal Auth. GetSecretVersionsAsync reads the current version and probes versions 1 through the current version, so it costs N + 1 API calls. Missing versions are skipped. Histories longer than 1000 versions are rejected to bound the request count. CreatedAt is null because the SDK does not expose secret timestamps. Metadata: SecretMetadata.Tags is stored as Infisical per-secret metadata. Infisical project tags are not supported because they require pre-created tag IDs. On update, null tags leave the existing metadata unchanged and an empty dictionary removes it. Infisical's create and update responses do not include metadata, so PutSecretAsync reports the tags that are now stored (the tags you sent, or the existing ones when you sent none). Secret keys: The SDK appends the key to the request path without escaping it. To avoid addressing the wrong secret or API route, keys that are empty, equal to . or .., or contain /, \, ? or # are rejected with SecretProviderException before any request is sent. Empty values: Infisical rejects empty secret values, so PutSecretAsync with an empty string throws SecretProviderException. Secret references: By default Infisical expands references such as ${OTHER_SECRET} when a secret is read, so a value written as pre-${OTHER_SECRET}-post is returned expanded by GetSecretAsync, while PutSecretAsync returns it as stored. Set ExpandSecretReferences to false to read back exactly what was written. Multi-line values: New and updated values are written with SkipMultilineEncoding = true so values round-trip unchanged. Values written by other clients with encoding enabled may be returned encoded. Stored values: PutSecretAsync returns the value stored by Infisical. Infisical may trim leading or trailing whitespace. Approval policies: Projects with secret approval policies may return an approval request instead of a secret. The provider reports this as an empty response; approval workflows are not supported. Imported secrets: The SDK includes imported secrets in list results. An imported key can be read but cannot be updated through this provider. Delete: DeleteSecretAsync permanently deletes the secret and throws SecretNotFoundException when the secret does not exist. Missing secrets: The SDK retries every failed GET request three times with 2, 4 and 8 second waits, so GetSecretAsync for a missing secret (or a missing version) takes about 14 seconds before SecretNotFoundException is thrown. SecretExistsAsync uses a list call and does not have this delay, so check it first when a secret may not exist. One environment and path: Each provider instance targets one project, environment and secret path. Create multiple providers to read from multiple environments or paths. TLS: The SDK does not expose an HTTP handler, so there is no SkipTlsVerify option. Use a certificate that the runtime trusts. Cancellation: The SDK does not accept a CancellationToken for its HTTP calls. The provider stops waiting when the token is cancelled, but the SDK request may continue in the background. Authentication methods: Only Universal Auth is supported. Token Auth, LDAP, cloud IAM and Kubernetes authentication are follow-ups.

Oracle Vault uses OCIDs (Oracle Cloud Identifiers) to reference secrets. The key parameter in all provider methods should be the full secret OCID: var secretOcid = "ocid1.vaultsecret.oc1.ap-mumbai-1.xxxxx"; var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync(secretOcid);

Oracle Vault maintains version history with numeric version numbers and named stages (CURRENT, PREVIOUS, PENDING): // Get all versions of a secret var versions = await provider.GetSecretVersionsAsync(secretOcid); foreach (var version in versions) { Console.WriteLine($"Version: {version.Version}"); Console.WriteLine($"Created: {version.CreatedAt}"); Console.WriteLine($"Current: {version.IsCurrent}"); } // Get a specific version by version number var query = new SecretQuery { Version = "2" }; var oldSecret = await provider.GetSecretAsync(secretOcid, query);

When calling PutSecretAsync, the provider automatically determines whether to create a new secret or update an existing one: New secret: Requires VaultId and CompartmentId to be configured Existing secret: Updates the current version automatically // Create or update a secret var result = await provider.PutSecretAsync(secretOcid, "my-secret-value"); // With metadata var metadata = new SecretMetadata { ContentType = "application/json", Tags = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["Environment"] = "Production", ["Owner"] = "Platform Team", } }; await provider.PutSecretAsync(secretOcid, "{\"key\":\"value\"}", metadata);

Oracle Vault uses soft-delete with scheduled deletion. When you call DeleteSecretAsync, the secret is marked for deletion but not immediately removed: await provider.DeleteSecretAsync(secretOcid); Soft Delete OCI Vault uses soft-delete by default. Deleted secrets can be recovered within the deletion window configured for your vault.

The Passbolt provider integrates with Passbolt, an open-source password and credential manager built for teams. It communicates via Passbolt's REST API using HttpClient with JWT-based authentication and OpenPGP end-to-end encryption. Key Benefits: Open-source and self-hosted End-to-end encryption using OpenPGP Team collaboration with granular sharing No vendor lock-in — you control your infrastructure JWT-based authentication (no session management needed)
Terminal dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.Passbolt

Option Type Required Default Description BaseUrl string Yes "" Base URL of the Passbolt instance UserPrivateKey string Yes "" User's private key, for authentication UserPrivateKeyPassphrase string Conditional "" Passphrase for the user's private key. Required only if the key is passphrase-protected UserKeyFingerprint string Yes "" Fingerprint of the user's public key PassboltOptions.Validate() requires BaseUrl, UserPrivateKey and UserKeyFingerprint.

Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPassbolt(options => { options.BaseUrl = "https://passbolt.example.com"; options.UserPrivateKey = "-----BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK-----\n..."; options.UserPrivateKeyPassphrase = "your-passphrase"; options.UserKeyFingerprint = "ABCDEF1234567890"; }) .Build();

Terminal export SECRETS_PROVIDER=passbolt export SECRETS_PASSBOLT_BASEURL=https://passbolt.example.com export SECRETS_PASSBOLT_USERPRIVATEKEY="-----BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK-----..." export SECRETS_PASSBOLT_USERPRIVATEPASSPHRASE=your-passphrase export SECRETS_PASSBOLT_USERKEYFINGERPRINT=ABCDEF1234567890

secretstore.yaml provider: passbolt: base: url: https://passbolt.example.com user: private: key: | -----BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK----- <your-armored-private-key> -----END PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK----- passphrase: your-passphrase key: fingerprint: ABCDEF1234567890

Bind the same settings from appsettings.json through the DI container: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .ConfigurePassbolt(configuration) .Build(); { "SecretsManager": { "Passbolt": { "BaseUrl": "https://passbolt.example.com", "UserPrivateKey": "-----BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK-----...", "UserKeyFingerprint": "ABCD1234..." } } } This reads from the SecretsManager:Passbolt section and validates all options.

Passbolt uses JWT-based authentication with OpenPGP end-to-end encryption. You'll need: Passbolt instance URL — the base URL of your Passbolt server User PGP private key — your armored OpenPGP private key (exported from the Passbolt extension or GnuPG) Private key passphrase — the passphrase that protects your private key Key fingerprint — your PGP key fingerprint (uppercase, no spaces)

Install the Passbolt browser extension and complete the setup Export your private key from the extension settings (Account > Export) Note your key fingerprint from the extension or Passbolt admin panel Use the exported key and fingerprint in your configuration warning Never commit your PGP private key or passphrase to version control. Use environment variables or a secrets manager for production deployments.

The provider maps Passbolt concepts to the ISecretProvider interface: ISecretProvider Passbolt Secret key Resource name Secret value Encrypted password field within the resource secret Metadata Resource metadata (username, uri, description) Version Not natively supported (single version returned)

Passbolt uses resource types to define the structure of secrets. The provider automatically discovers the password-and-description resource type on first use. This type stores the secret value in an encrypted password field.

All secrets are encrypted client-side using your PGP key before being sent to the Passbolt server. The server never sees the plaintext value. When retrieving secrets, the encrypted data is decrypted locally using your private key.

// Standard ISecretProvider operations work identically var secret = await provider.GetSecretAsync("my-secret"); await provider.PutSecretAsync("new-secret", "secret-value"); var versions = await provider.GetSecretVersionsAsync("my-secret"); await provider.DeleteSecretAsync("old-secret"); Versioning Passbolt does not support native secret versioning. Each update replaces the previous secret value. GetSecretVersionsAsync always returns a single version marked as current.

The PostgreSQL provider stores secrets in a PostgreSQL database with optional AES-256-GCM encryption at rest. It uses Npgsql with raw SQL for lightweight, direct database access -- no ORM overhead. Key Benefits: Use your existing PostgreSQL infrastructure for secrets AES-256-GCM encryption at rest (optional) Auto-versioning with per-secret version history Optional table auto-creation, with an ownership check on the tables it uses Tags stored as JSONB for flexible querying
Terminal dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager dotnet add package mrhamburg.SecretsManager.PostgreSql

Option Type Required Default Description ConnectionString string Yes "" PostgreSQL connection string, e.g. Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=pass Schema string No "public" Database schema for the tables TablePrefix string No "sm_" Prefix for table names, to avoid collisions AutoCreateSchema bool No false Create the tables automatically on first use. Requires CREATE on the schema SchemaOwner string? No null Role expected to own the secrets tables. When null, the connected role must own them EncryptionKey string? No null Base64-encoded AES-256 key (32 bytes). When set, values are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM EncryptionKeyFile string? No null Path to a file containing the encryption key. A 32-byte file is used as-is, otherwise it is treated as base64 EncryptionKeyProvider IEncryptionKeyProvider? No null Supplies the encryption key from an external source, for example another secret provider. Fluent API only — it is an object, so it cannot come from appsettings.json, YAML, or an environment variable PostgreSqlOptions.Validate() requires ConnectionString, rejects EncryptionKey, EncryptionKeyFile and EncryptionKeyProvider being set together, and caps TablePrefix at 40 characters (PostgreSQL truncates identifiers at 63 bytes, which can collapse the two table names into one). Validation runs on every construction path.

Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; options.Schema = "public"; options.TablePrefix = "sm_"; options.EncryptionKey = "base64-encoded-32-byte-key"; }) .Build();

The key can be held in a different secret provider entirely — Azure Key Vault, Scaleway, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or any of the other providers. It is fetched on first use and cached per key version. Program.cs // The bootstrap provider holds the key. It is built first and owned by the caller. await using var keyProvider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithAzureKeyVault(options => options.VaultUri = "https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/") .Build(); await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; options.EncryptionKeyProvider = new SecretProviderKeySource(keyProvider, "sm-data-key"); }) .Build(); Store the key as base64 — openssl rand -base64 32 — and rotate it by putting a new version of that secret. The current key is cached per process: new writes pick up the new version on restart, or immediately if you call InvalidateKey(). Existing rows stay readable either way, because each row records the key version it was written with and GetKeyAsync fetches that exact version on demand. The same pattern works with Scaleway: await using var keyProvider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithScaleway(options => { options.Region = "fr-par"; options.ProjectId = "..."; options.AccessKey = "..."; options.SecretKey = "..."; }) .Build(); await using var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; options.EncryptionKeyProvider = new SecretProviderKeySource(keyProvider, "sm/data-key"); }) .Build(); warning Build the key provider first, and never point a key source at the store it encrypts. A self-referential key source recurses or fails on first use — the fetch happens inside the operation that needs the key, so it cannot bootstrap itself. SecretProviderKeySource does not dispose the provider it wraps. The caller owns the bootstrap provider and may use it for other keys. tip Call WarmUpAsync() to resolve the key and ensure the schema at startup rather than on the first read or write. Without it, a misconfigured key source surfaces only when the first secret is accessed.

documents.t: Terminal export SECRETS_PROVIDER=postgresql export SECRETS_POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING="Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret" export SECRETS_POSTGRESQL_SCHEMA=public export SECRETS_POSTGRESQL_TABLE_PREFIX=sm_ export SECRETS_POSTGRESQL_AUTO_CREATE_SCHEMA=true export SECRETS_POSTGRESQL_ENCRYPTION_KEY=base64encodedkey

Bind the same settings from appsettings.json through the DI container: var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .ConfigurePostgreSql(configuration) .Build(); { "SecretsManager": { "PostgreSql": { "ConnectionString": "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=pass" } } } This reads from the SecretsManager:PostgreSql section and validates all options.

The same package also ships a PostgreSQL-backed audit sink, so secret access records can live in the database you already operate: Program.cs var provider = new SecretProviderBuilder() .WithPostgreSql(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=secret"; }) .WithPostgreSqlAuditSink(options => { options.ConnectionString = "Host=localhost;Database=secrets;Username=audit_app;Password=secret"; options.Schema = "public"; options.TableName = "sm_secret_audit_log"; }) .Build(); Option Type Required Default Description ConnectionString string Yes "" PostgreSQL connection string Schema string No "public" Schema for the audit table TableName string No "sm_secret_audit_log" Audit table name (48 characters or fewer, so the generated index name fits) AutoCreateSchema bool No false Create the table and timestamp index on first write. Requires CREATE on the schema The sink writes one row per audited operation. It stores the operation, provider, key, version, outcome, timestamp, duration, actor, correlation id, trace id, and failure type. It never stores a secret value. See Audit Trail for the table schema, failure semantics, and actor propagation.

Npgsql defaults to SslMode=Prefer, which permits an unencrypted connection and does not verify the server certificate. Add SSL Mode=VerifyFull to the connection string in any environment that is not a trusted local socket: Host=db.example.com;Database=secrets;Username=app;Password=...;SSL Mode=VerifyFull Without it, the database password, secret keys, tags and any unencrypted values can be read or modified in transit.

AutoCreateSchema defaults to false so the runtime account does not need CREATE on the schema. Create the tables from a migration role and grant the application only DML rights on the two tables: CREATE SCHEMA secrets AUTHORIZATION secrets_owner; REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA secrets FROM PUBLIC; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA secrets TO secrets_app; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON secrets.sm_secrets, secrets.sm_secret_versions TO secrets_app; GRANT USAGE ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA secrets TO secrets_app; options.AutoCreateSchema = false; // the migration role creates the tables options.SchemaOwner = "secrets_owner"; // the app connects as secrets_app When AutoCreateSchema is true, the provider checks pg_class.relowner for both tables after the DDL and throws if the owner is not SchemaOwner (or the connected role when it is unset). A role that can create objects in the target schema could otherwise create the tables first, own them, and read every secret written afterwards — or add a trigger that copies values elsewhere.

When EncryptionKey or EncryptionKeyFile is configured, secret values are encrypted before storage using AES-256-GCM. Encrypted values are stored as JSON in the value column: {"n":"<nonce-base64>","c":"<ciphertext-base64>","t":"<tag-base64>"} Each version row has an encrypted boolean column. The provider refuses to mix the two states: a row marked unencrypted while a key is configured, or an encrypted row with no key configured, both throw SecretProviderException. This closes the downgrade attack — UPDATE ... SET encrypted = false, value = 'attacker-value', which anyone with database access could otherwise use to forge a secret such as a connection string pointing at their own server. It also means a key cannot simply be added to a database that already holds plaintext rows; those rows must be rewritten. tip Generate a 32-byte encryption key with: openssl rand -base64 32
The provider creates two tables (auto-created when AutoCreateSchema is true):

Column Type Description id SERIAL Primary key key TEXT UNIQUE Secret identifier content_type TEXT MIME type (nullable) tags JSONB Key-value metadata (nullable) created_at TIMESTAMPTZ Creation timestamp updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ Last update timestamp

Column Type Description id SERIAL Primary key secret_id INTEGER FK to secrets table (cascade delete) version INTEGER Auto-incrementing version per secret value TEXT Secret value (encrypted or plaintext) encrypted BOOLEAN Whether the value is encrypted created_at TIMESTAMPTZ Creation timestamp is_current BOOLEAN Whether this is the latest version

Key Benefits: Fully managed by Tencent Cloud Server-side encryption with KMS-managed keys Automatic version rotation for secrets Integrated with other Tencent Cloud services Regional availability across global Tencent Cloud data centers

Log in to the Tencent Cloud Console Navigate to API Key Management (API Gateway or Tencent Cloud Console settings) Create or select an API key Ensure the key has permissions for Secrets Manager operations warning Never commit your SecretKey to version control. Use environment variables or a secrets manager for production deployments.

The provider maps Tencent Cloud Secrets Manager concepts to the ISecretProvider interface: ISecretProvider Tencent Cloud Secret key Secret name Secret value SecretValue (server-side encrypted) Version VersionId (UUID-based, auto-generated) Metadata Not directly mapped

Tencent Cloud Secrets Manager supports up to 10 versions per secret. When the limit is reached, the oldest version is automatically deleted in a rolling manner. Each version is labeled with Latest (current) or Previous (older).

All secret values are encrypted server-side by KMS using a symmetric key. The encryption is transparent — you work with plaintext values, and Tencent Cloud handles encryption/decryption automatically.
